summary: This Wikipedia article covers Saint Helena, a volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic and British Overseas Territory. It describes its sports and telecommunications infrastructure, a long history of emigration and population decline, and its colonial history from English East India Company settlement in 1659 through slavery and later labour. It also touches on media, a 2010s child abuse controversy, and the island's strong royal loyalty.
one_line: Overview of Saint Helena, a remote South Atlantic British territory covering its history, sports, media, emigration and population.
key_facts: Saint Helena is a volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean, 4,000 kilometres east of Rio de Janeiro.
Saint Helena has a population of 4,255 according to the 2008 census.
The island was named after Saint Helena of Constantinople.
Oliver Cromwell granted the English East India Company a charter to govern Saint Helena in 1657.
The first governor, Captain John Dutton, arrived on Saint Helena in 1659.
The fort on the island was renamed James Fort and the town Jamestown, in honour of the Duke of York, later James II of England.
The importation of slaves to St Helena was banned in 1792, and phased emancipation of over 800 resident slaves did not take place until 1827.
The British Nationality Act 1981 reclassified Saint Helena as a British Dependent Territory, and islanders lost their right of abode in Britain.
Saints were re-awarded UK citizenship in 2002, and emigration to the UK by a wider range of wage-earners accelerated afterward.
The population dropped from 5,157 at the 1998 census to 4,255 in 2008.
Edmond Halley set up an astronomical observatory on Saint Helena in 1676 with a 7.3-metre-long aerial telescope.
The 680-metre high hill near the observatory site is named Halley's Mount.
The Governor's Cup is a yacht race between Cape Town and Saint Helena, held every two years in December/January.
The island has a single satellite ground station at The Briars providing the only international connection via Intelsat 707.
King George VI is the only reigning monarch to have visited the island, in 1947.
